$comment: The remaining California wage, hour, and leave obligations. Most of these are small individually and none of them are optional; they matter because each is PAGA-enforceable per employee per pay period.

clauses.title: Day of Rest
clauses.rationale: The entitlement is measured per workweek rather than on a rolling seven-day basis, and an employer may not cause an employee to forgo it — an employee may choose to work, but only if genuinely informed and uncoerced.
clauses.body: Employees are entitled to one [[day of rest|day of rest]] in seven, measured by the workweek. The exemption for weeks in which no day exceeds six hours applies only where that is true of every day in the week. An employee may choose to work a seventh day if fully apprised of the entitlement, but the Company may not induce or pressure that choice. Seventh-day work also carries the overtime and double time premiums in <<xr:hb_ca_overtime>>.

clauses.title: On-Call, Travel, and Control Time
clauses.rationale: California uses a control test rather than the narrower federal standard, so time that is unpaid under federal law is frequently compensable here — including time spent under employer control before the shift formally begins.
clauses.body: Hours worked in California means all time an employee is subject to the Company's control, which is broader than the federal standard. Compensable time includes required travel between worksites, time spent under control before a shift formally begins such as mandatory security or bag checks, and on-call time where the constraints are restrictive enough that the employee cannot use the period effectively for their own purposes. Ordinary commuting is not compensable, but travel in a required employer vehicle usually is. Sleep time cannot be excluded from a shift of under twenty-four hours.

clauses.title: Uniforms, Tools, and Equipment
clauses.rationale: A deposit or deduction for equipment is unlawful even with the employee's written agreement, which is the part employers most often get wrong.
clauses.body: Where the Company requires a uniform, it must provide and maintain it at its own expense. Required tools and equipment must be provided by the Company unless the employee earns at least twice the minimum wage and the tools are those customary in the trade. The Company may not require a deposit, take a deduction, or condition final pay on return of equipment — even with written consent. Recovering the value of unreturned property is a separate civil matter, not a payroll deduction.

clauses.title: Suitable Seating
clauses.benchmark: A frequent PAGA claim in retail and customer-facing roles
clauses.rationale: An obscure wage order provision that generates a steady volume of representative claims, because the analysis is task-by-task rather than role-by-role.
clauses.body: Employees shall be provided suitable seating where the nature of the work reasonably permits it, assessed by the tasks performed at a given location rather than by the job title as a whole. Where work must be done standing, adequate seating shall be placed nearby for use when it does not interfere with the work. This is a wage order requirement enforceable through PAGA under <<xr:can_paga>>.

clauses.title: Jury, Witness, and Voting Leave
clauses.rationale: Small entitlements with real teeth: discipline for jury service is a misdemeanor, and the voting notice has a posting requirement most employers miss entirely.
clauses.body: The Company will not discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to serve as required by law on an inquest or trial jury, where the employee gives reasonable notice before taking the time off, or for taking time off to appear in court under a subpoena or other court order as a witness. Neither protection is a right to be paid, and neither is a grant of leave: Labor Code section 230 does not require an employer to compensate time taken off for jury service, and it does not reach time off taken when the employee is not actually serving. An employee may use accrued vacation, personal leave or compensatory time off for the absence, and that entitlement cannot be reduced by a collective bargaining agreement. An exempt employee is a separate case: under the federal salary-basis rule an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which they perform any work, without regard to days or hours worked, subject to the deductions that rule allows — including a deduction for a full-day absence taken for personal reasons other than sickness or disability. Voting leave is a different statute. A voter without sufficient time outside working hours to vote at a statewide election may take enough working time to vote, of which no more than two (2) hours is without loss of pay, at the beginning or end of the shift unless otherwise mutually agreed; an employee who knows on the third working day before the election that they will need the time must give at least two (2) working days' notice. Not less than ten (10) days before every statewide election, post a notice setting out Elections Code section 14000 where employees can see it, and do not ask an employee to bring a vote-by-mail ballot to work or to vote it at work.

eCFR (Office of the Federal Register) — 29 C.F.R. §541.602, salary basis

defects: The previous citation was "Cal. Lab. Code §§230, 14350–14353". There is no Labor Code §14350; the voting leave provisions are Elections Code §§14000–14004. Every voting assertion in the clause was cited to a section of the wrong code, and the exempt-salary assertion was cited to the Labor Code when it comes from a federal regulation. Both have been re-cited.

Labor Code §230 also protects a victim of crime or abuse who takes time off for relief or to appear, and requires reasonable accommodation for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Those subdivisions were read and are not carried here because the corpus has a separate hb_ca_victim_leave clause, which was not examined for this rebuild and may or may not state them correctly.
The clause says nothing about how a voting-leave dispute is enforced. Elections Code §§14000–14004 carry no express remedy that was found in the text read, and none was researched.

clauses.title: School and Child Care Activity Leave
clauses.rationale: Attaches by worksite headcount rather than company headcount, which means a company can be covered at one location and not another.
clauses.body: Where the Company has twenty-five (25) or more employees at the same location, a parent, guardian, or grandparent with custody may take up to forty (40) hours per year, capped at eight (8) hours per month, to find, enroll, or participate in activities of a child's school or licensed child care. Additional unpaid time is available for a school-directed appearance or a child care emergency. Employees may use accrued paid leave. Coverage is measured per worksite, not company-wide.

clauses.title: Military and Military Spouse Leave
clauses.rationale: California adds a spousal leave entitlement on top of federal USERRA reemployment rights, and it attaches at a low headcount.
clauses.body: Provide leave and reinstatement rights for military service under federal USERRA and California law, including protection against discrimination for service obligations. Separately, where the Company has twenty-five (25) or more employees, provide up to ten (10) days of unpaid leave to the spouse or registered domestic partner of a service member on leave from deployment during a period of military conflict.

clauses.title: Crime Victim and Safety Leave
clauses.rationale: The confidentiality and accommodation duties are as important as the leave itself, and the entitlement now reaches family members of victims rather than only victims.
clauses.body: Provide time off for an employee who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or another qualifying crime — and for a family member of a victim — to obtain relief, seek medical attention, or access services. Employees may use accrued paid leave. Provide reasonable safety accommodations such as a schedule or workspace change on request. Keep all related information confidential except as required by law, and do not discriminate or retaliate. Notice of these rights must be given at hire and on request.

clauses.title: Organ and Bone Marrow Donor Leave
clauses.rationale: Paid leave, which is unusual among California entitlements, and it may not be run concurrently with FMLA or CFRA.
clauses.body: Where the Company has fifteen (15) or more employees, provide up to thirty (30) business days of paid leave in a twelve-month period for organ donation and up to five (5) business days for bone marrow donation, plus an equal period of unpaid leave for organ donation. The Company may require the employee to use a limited amount of accrued leave first. This leave does not run concurrently with FMLA or CFRA and the employee must be restored to the same position.

clauses.title: Lactation Breaks
clauses.rationale: Denial carries the same one-hour premium as a missed rest period and is separately PAGA-enforceable, so it compounds the same way.
clauses.body: You are entitled to a reasonable amount of break time each time you need to express milk for your infant child. Where possible it runs at the same time as a break you already get; break time that does not run concurrently with your authorized paid rest time is unpaid. The Company does not have to provide the break time where doing so would seriously disrupt its operations. You are entitled to a private space that is not a bathroom and that meets the requirements in <<xr:can_lactation>>, and to a written response if the Company cannot provide the break time or a compliant space. An employer with fewer than fifty (50) employees may be excused from a particular requirement if it can show that requirement would cause undue hardship, judged against the size, resources, nature and structure of the business; even then, if the space requirement is what causes the hardship, it must still make reasonable efforts to give you somewhere other than a toilet stall, close to where you work. If you are denied the break time or adequate space, you are owed one (1) additional hour of pay on the same basis as a missed rest period under <<xr:hb_meal_rest>>, you may complain to the Labor Commissioner, and the Labor Commissioner may impose a civil penalty of one hundred dollars ($100) for each day you were denied it. The Company will not discharge you, discriminate against you or retaliate against you for asking for or using this accommodation.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §§1030, 1031, 1032, 1033 and 1034
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §226.7

defects: The clause tells the employee they are owed an hour of pay "on the same basis as a missed rest period", and hb_meal_rest now carries Ferra's construction of that measure. If hb_meal_rest is ever edited without this clause being re-read, the cross-reference will silently carry whatever hb_meal_rest then says.
No decision construing §§1030–1034 was found. The §1032 "seriously disrupt the operations" exception is stated to the employee with no gloss on what it means, because nothing read here supplies one.
The clause states the §226.7 premium and the §1033(c) civil penalty together without saying whether both are available for the same denial. That was not researched.

clauses.title: Tips and Service Charges
clauses.benchmark: Relevant wherever any percentage-based charge appears on a customer invoice
clauses.rationale: California allows no tip credit at all, and a mandatory service charge is not a tip — it belongs to the employer unless represented otherwise, which creates its own exposure.
clauses.body: California permits no tip credit: employees must receive the full minimum wage regardless of tips. Tips belong to the employee and may not be taken by the Company or by any owner, manager, or supervisor, and the Company may not deduct credit card processing fees from them. Tip pooling among employees in the chain of service is permitted. A mandatory service charge is not a tip and belongs to the Company unless it has been represented otherwise to the customer — but several local ordinances require service charges to be distributed to the workers who performed the service.
